name: asmlib (abiiranathan): AVX2/BMI2 and NEON assembly libc string and memory routines
language: x86-64 assembly (NASM) with AArch64 assembly and C
baseline: glibc 2.44 memcpy, memset, memcmp, strlen, memchr, strstr, memmem and strcmp (libc routines called through volatile function pointers)
workload: bench/bench.c (make bench) measures nanoseconds per call at several sizes with 20000 iterations per size for memcpy, memset, memcmp, strlen, memchr and strstr against glibc; the README reports the outcome per routine.
claimed_speedup: memchr 'consistently faster (about 1.1-1.2x from 128 bytes up)'; mid/large memcpy, memset and memcmp 'at parity (about 0.95-1.2x)'; memmem 'several times faster than libc's'; strcmp/strncmp 'faster than glibc's two-way strcmp'. Losses stated by the author: strlen about 0.5-0.8x under 64 KiB and strstr about 0.4-0.65x versus glibc.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.2.1 and Clang 22.1.8; Makefile default CFLAGS ?= -O2 -Wall -Wextra; libc and asmlib entry points held in volatile function pointers so the compiler cannot substitute builtins (docs/BENCHMARKS.md).
hardware: Intel Core i7-10510U (Comet Lake), 4 cores / 8 threads, AVX2 + BMI1 + BMI2 + ERMS + FMA, Linux 7.2.
tradeoffs: Requires an x86-64 CPU with AVX2 and BMI1 (with a documented scalar fallback build) or an AArch64 CPU; exposes an asm_* API in asmlib.h rather than overriding libc symbols; routines are page-boundary safe by design; the repo also bundles arena allocator, malloc, math and printf/scanf replacements that are outside this category.
caveats: Repository is only weeks old (first commit 2026-09-27). docs/BENCHMARKS.md says the memory and string results are 'reported qualitatively' because laptop turbo and thermal state swing absolute numbers, so the ratios above come from the README prose, not a fixed table. Single laptop CPU. glibc keeps an edge on strlen and strstr. Parity results for memcpy, memset and memcmp mean no practical gain there. Already reported by a sibling search under hand-written-asm-kernels.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com only): 'faster than glibc strlen memcpy memcmp strcmp implementation AVX2 NEON README benchmark results'; opened README.md, docs/BENCHMARKS.md and Makefile

name: memx (Rust memchr, memmem, memcmp, memcpy, memset)
baseline: libc memchr, memmem, memcmp, memcpy and memset as shipped by glibc (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and musl (x86_64-unknown-linux-musl), called through the libc crate; the same bench also lists Rust std equivalents and the memchr crate
workload: Per-function benchmark over an English-text haystack (short) and a Japanese-text haystack (long), run for the gnu and musl targets; the table reports time per benchmark run in microseconds (lower is better), with SSE2 and AVX2 variants of each memx function listed separately.
claimed_speedup: memmem on i5-4570: memx 0.798/1.230 us (gnu en/ja) vs libc 2.173/3.828 us, and 0.794/1.197 us (musl en/ja) vs libc 3.948/7.010 us, i.e. about 2.7x, 3.1x, 5.0x and 5.9x (derived from page data). memchr: memx 4.451/5.402 us vs libc 4.849/5.764 us on glibc (about 1.1x) and 4.426/5.322 us vs libc 8.757/10.205 us on musl (about 2.0x, derived from page data). Not uniformly faster: memcmp, memcpy and memset on glibc are slower than libc in several cells (memcpy gnu:en 7.016 us vs 3.483 us, memset gnu:en 3.388 us vs 2.003 us, memcmp gnu:en 2.828 us vs 1.584 us).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.69.0 (84c898d65 2023-04-16); Cargo.toml [profile.bench] opt-level = 3, codegen-units = 1, lto = true; benchmark harness lives in the xbench workspace member.
hardware: Intel Core i5-4570 @ 3.2 GHz (x86_64 gnu and musl targets); also Intel Q6600 @ 2.40 GHz (x86_64, i686, i586) and an armv7 1.5 GHz device in the memchr table.
tradeoffs: Rust crate (no_std capable); SSE2 and AVX2 kernels on x86 and x86_64 only, other targets use a basic word-at-a-time path. A separate crate, memx-cdy (github.com/aki-akaguma/memx-cdy), exposes a C ABI and an LD_PRELOAD shim, but its README gives no numbers of its own. memcmp, memcpy and memset do not beat glibc on the author's Haswell-class machine, so the win is concentrated in memmem and in memchr against musl.
caveats: Hardware is a 2013 desktop CPU and a 2007 Core 2 Quad, with rustc 1.69.0 (2023); results are per-run totals on two author-chosen text corpora whose sizes are not stated in the README. The speedup on musl partly reflects musl's generic C routines being slow. Several functions (memcmp, memcpy, memset) are slower than libc in the gnu columns, so only memmem and memchr are real wins. No modern x86 or aarch64 server numbers.
found_via: WebSearch of crates.io API (q=memcmp, q=memrchr) surfaced the crate; opened github.com/aki-akaguma/memx and docs/README.memchr.md, README.memcmp.md, README.memcpy.md, README.memmem.md, README.memset.md

language: Rust (C ABI shared and static library, LD_PRELOAD capable)
baseline: glibc and musl libc memchr, memmem, memcmp, memcpy and memset (called from Rust through FFI as libc_* rows), alongside Rust std and the memchr crate

tradeoffs: Rust implementation with SSE2/AVX2 paths selected at run time (cpufeatures) plus a basic fallback; usable from C or C++ by linking libmemx_cdy.a/.so or LD_PRELOAD, but it needs a Rust toolchain to build and the Rust side must call memx_init(). Substantially slower than glibc for memcmp, memcpy and memset on the same CPU, so only the search functions (memmem, memchr on musl) are wins.
caveats: First-party benchmarks on a 2013-era desktop CPU with rustc 1.69; the libc_* rows are libc functions called through Rust FFI. memx's own harness shows the memchr crate's memmem about 4x slower than glibc memmem (9.127 vs 2.173 us), which contradicts the memchr author's rebar results, so the harness probably builds a searcher on every call and the memmem gap should be treated with care. Single table per function, no repeat statistics. The benchmark code and docs live in the memx repository, not memx-cdy.

claimed_speedup: FindLongestCommonSuffix 6.87x (full match 4096 B 1524 ns to 233 ns, 6.5x; 256 B 6.9x); memcasecmp 5.98x (eq_case 256 B 229 ns to 38 ns; 4096 B eq_exact 4.99x, eq_case 5.82x); RemoveExtraAsciiWhitespace 1.40x on already-clean input

hardware: Apple M2, macOS 24.5

name: rvv-bench (RISC-V Vector memcpy, memset and strlen assembly)
language: Assembly (RISC-V Vector 1.0) with a C harness
baseline: libc memcpy, memset and strlen of the benchmarked RISC-V board (hosted libc, version not stated); the same harness also times musl's C memcpy/strlen, a byte-wise scalar loop and a compiler auto-vectorized scalar loop
workload: Bytes per cycle (hardware cycle counter) of memcpy (random misalignment and aligned), memset and strlen for sizes from 1 byte to tens of MB, comparing hand-written RVV assembly variants (LMUL m1 to m8, aligned, tail-handling and vlmax strategies) with libc, musl and scalar code.
claimed_speedup: No headline number in the README; the numbers are in the per-board results pages. Derived from page data (SpacemiT X60 results, one fixed variant rvv_m4 against libc, bytes/cycle at the nearest recorded size): memcpy 4.73x at about 66 B (1.941 vs 0.410), 2.71x at about 1 KB (4.298 vs 1.585), 2.71x at about 16 KB (5.040 vs 1.860), 2.05x at about 265 KB (3.438 vs 1.674); memset 3.55x at about 66 B, 1.64x at about 1 KB, 1.72x at about 16 KB, 1.79x at about 265 KB; strlen 1.36x at about 61 B, 1.81x at about 1 KB, 2.44x at about 16 KB, 2.89x at about 260 KB. Picking the best variant per size gives up to 4.9x for strlen at 16 KB (rvv_page_aligned_m8 6.388 vs libc 1.308 B/cycle).
compiler_and_flags: config.mk default: cc -march=rv64gcv -O3 -Wall -Wextra -DUSE_PERF_EVENT (native build; the compiler name and version are not stated in the files opened; the results page labels the compiler auto-vectorized scalar row 'scalar_autovec_clang18')
hardware: SpacemiT X60 (SpacemiT K1, Banana Pi BPI-F3) for the figures quoted; the results repository also has folders for SiFive P870, XuanTie C920V2, SpacemiT A100 and X100, Tenstorrent X280, Sipeed Lichee Pi 4A, CanMV K230 and others
tradeoffs: RISC-V Vector 1.0 hardware only (rv64gcv); an XTheadVector instruction-timing directory exists but the README says it is no longer maintained. The kernels are benchmark implementations in bench/*.S, meant to be studied or copied rather than a drop-in libc; the best variant (LMUL, alignment strategy) differs per core, and the page-aligned strlen needs the page size to be known.
caveats: The baseline is whatever libc the board runs (version not recorded; most likely a scalar glibc or musl without an RVV path), so part of the gap is the absence of RVV code in libc, not a better algorithm. Ratios were derived by the reporter from the chart data embedded in the results HTML at the nearest recorded size, for one fixed variant; the best-variant-per-size figure is a selection. Single run per size, no error bars. The rendered results site is on github.io (blocked here), so the HTML in the rvv-bench-results repository was parsed. Other kernels in the repo (utf8_count, memreverse, mergelines, byteswap, base64) have no libc counterpart and are not part of this claim.

name: sve-string-routines-benchmarks (Arm SVE strcpy, strncpy, strcmp, strncmp)
language: Assembly (AArch64 SVE) with a C harness
baseline: GNU libc 2.39 string routines (strcpy, strncpy, strcmp, strncmp, strlen, memcpy as selected on Graviton3E) and the Arm Optimized Routines 23.01 SVE versions
workload: Median per-call runtime (101 samples, warmed-up hot-cache loops) and bandwidth of string routines on random alphanumeric buffers: short strings 1 to 128 B in steps of 1, and 128 B to 512 MiB doubling, aligned and unaligned allocations, on an AWS Graviton3E.
claimed_speedup: README: the proposed SVE implementations 'never' regress against Arm optimized-routines and 'are competitive with their GNU libc counterparts, namely: strcpy, strncpy, strcmp and strncmp'. Derived from page data (raw .dat median runtimes, glibc 2.39 time divided by proposed time, geometric mean over buffer sizes, aligned/unaligned): 128 B to 512 MiB strcpy 1.64x/1.61x, strncpy 1.40x/1.39x, strcmp 1.37x/1.32x, strncmp 1.45x/1.43x; 1 to 128 B strncpy 1.63x/1.58x, strcpy 1.32x/1.13x, strncmp 1.19x/1.18x, strcmp 1.13x/1.13x. Against Arm optimized-routines 23.01 at 128 B to 512 MiB (derived): strcpy 2.8x, strlen 3.0x, strcmp 1.8x. The README lists memcpy, memcmp, strlen, strnlen, strchr and strrchr as inconclusive (memcpy geomean 0.76x of glibc at full sizes, strlen 0.94x).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.3.0 on kernel 6.2.0-1018-aws; CMake C11 build with no explicit optimization flag (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release is commented out in CMakeLists.txt); the measured routines are hand-written .S files, so the driver flags matter little; -DSHORT_STRS, -DFULL_SIZE_RANGE, -DALIGNED_ALLOCS and -DCMP_LIBC select the modes
hardware: AWS Graviton3E (hpc7g.16xlarge, Neoverse V1 with SVE); the latest commit message says NVIDIA Grace results were added (results/raw/Grace folder exists, not read)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; research project of UVSQ LI-PaRAD with SiPearl and Eviden (EMOPASS); the authors say it is worth merging into Arm optimized-routines and glibc
tradeoffs: AArch64 with SVE only (Neoverse V1/V2, A64FX, Grace). The change replaces INCx loop-offset increments with CNTx plus ADD and drops FFR-dependent instructions in the full-vector path; it needs one more register. Some unaligned short-string lengths are slower than glibc (strcpy ratio down to 0.37x at one size, strcmp down to 0.55x). The code is a benchmark harness with the routines under string/aarch64/new, not a packaged library.
caveats: Benchmark is by the authors of the new routines (research group, not independent). Hot-cache repeated calls with warm-up, so cold-cache and branch-predictor effects are not covered. glibc 2.39 runs its own NEON/generic implementations on Graviton3E (the README mentions the NEON strcmp), not SVE ones. The ratios are derived by the reporter from results/raw/G3E/*/*.dat; the README itself only gives qualitative statements and plots. One line in the unaligned full-range strncpy data file is malformed (23 of 24 sizes usable).

name: WojciechMula/toys avx512-string (AVX512F strlen, strchr, strrchr, strcmp)
baseline: libc strlen/strchr/strrchr/strcmp via <cstring> (labelled 'std' in the harness; libc version not stated)

name: tinymembench (NEON, prefetching and SSE2 copy and fill kernels against libc memcpy and memset)
language: C and assembly (ARM, AArch64, x86 SSE2, MIPS)
baseline: the libc memcpy and memset ('standard memcpy', 'standard memset') of each tested board's OS image
workload: Sequential copy and fill bandwidth on large aligned blocks, reporting MB/s for libc memcpy and memset next to C, NEON, VFP, ARM LDM/STM, SSE2 and non-temporal copy and fill kernels with different prefetch strategies; the wiki holds 68 community-submitted boards and PCs.
claimed_speedup: No headline claim; results are per-board wiki tables. Examples (ratios derived from page data): BeagleBone Black (Cortex-A8 AM3358 at 1 GHz): standard memcpy 258.3 MB/s vs 'C copy prefetched (32 bytes step)' 505.1 MB/s (1.96x) and 'NEON copy prefetched (32 bytes step)' 563.5 MB/s (2.18x); Allwinner A13: 249.8 vs 406.5 MB/s (1.63x). Intel Core i7-8700T: standard memcpy 16647.8 vs 'SSE2 nontemporal copy' 17273.1 MB/s (1.04x), standard memset 32815.6 vs 'SSE2 nontemporal fill' 41097.4 MB/s (1.25x). Raspberry Pi (BCM2835): libc memcpy 387.6 MB/s is level with the best custom copy (392.6 MB/s) and libc memset 1458.5 MB/s beats the custom fills.
compiler_and_flags: Not recorded on the wiki pages; the readme.txt build examples use CFLAGS=-O2 with a per-board -mcpu (for example -mcpu=cortex-a9, -mcpu=cortex-a8 -static)
hardware: Per wiki page: ARM Cortex-A8 AM3358 at 1 GHz (BeagleBone Black), Allwinner A13, Intel Core i7-8700T (6 cores, DDR4-2666), Raspberry Pi BCM2835 and 60+ other boards and PCs
stars_or_usage: 418 stars; a sibling report says amd/aocl-libmem bundles it in its benchmark tooling
tradeoffs: A benchmark program rather than a library: the kernels (arm-neon.S, aarch64-asm.S, x86-sse2.S, mips-32.S) are bandwidth tests on aligned blocks, not memcpy replacements (no small-size, misalignment or overlap handling). Prefetch distance is tuned per core, and non-temporal stores avoid cache pollution at the price of making later reads of the copy slow.
caveats: The ARM wins come from 2013 to 2017 era boards and are measured against whatever libc memcpy those OS images shipped (likely older glibc builds without NEON or prefetching copy loops, but the wiki records neither libc versions nor compiler flags), so they may not hold for current glibc, Bionic or Arm optimized-routines. On modern x86 desktops libc memcpy is within a few percent of the best custom kernel. Wiki runs come from many contributors with different OS images and tinymembench versions (v0.2.9 to v0.4.9). Results are large-block bandwidth, not small-copy latency. The code repository has had no commit since February 2017, although the wiki still receives runs (Ryzen 9800X3D, Core i9-13900K pages).

name: copies-and-fills (libcofi_rpi.so)
baseline: generic libc memcpy and memset on Raspberry Pi (ARM)
workload: Modified ssvb-membench with random numbers, iterating over sizes and source/destination alignments; memcpy and memset on a Raspberry Pi.
claimed_speedup: memcpy reaches performance parity with generic libc at around ~150 byte copies and 'eventually gains 2-3x throughput, especially when the source buffer is uncached' (up to 680 MB/s, effective 339 MB/s copy); memset reaches parity at around 100 bytes and peaks at 1390 MB/s, '~7x faster than the libc version'

The README says the library only reaches parity with libc at 100-150 bytes, so small copies gain nothing. The ~7x memset figure is a peak MB/s compared to libc, not a general average. Licence is stated as LGPL version 2.1 without 'or later'. Last commit 2012-08-03 and the hardware is obsolete.

name: KmStrSearch (Windows kernel UTF-8 and UTF-16 substring search)
baseline: Windows kernel CRT strstr and wcsstr (MSVC runtime; not glibc or musl)
workload: Single match near the end of a buffer (40 B to 1 MB for 8-bit, 80 B to 2 MB for 16-bit) and a worst-case mismatched dense text (repetitive partial matches), run through a multi-threaded kernel driver harness; hybrid Boyer-Moore-Horspool with SWAR, AVX2 and AVX-512BW engines versus CRT.
claimed_speedup: i7-1165G7, 8-bit, GB/s (CRT baseline vs Smart Auto): 10 KB 22.38 vs 45.71, 1 MB 22.66 vs 85.93; 16-bit 20 KB 26.67 vs 68.43. Worse on small buffers: 40 B 3.61 vs 1.95, 256 B 15.03 vs 4.88. README: on mismatched dense text CRT collapses to 0.21-0.37 GB/s while the hybrid delivers 49-81 GB/s, 'up to 385x faster'.
tradeoffs: Windows kernel-mode (WDK driver) code: routes small buffers to a SWAR path to avoid the KeSaveExtendedProcessorState cost of entering vector mode, and uses AVX2/AVX-512BW or ARM64 NEON for larger buffers. Uses 8 KB (UTF-16) skip tables allocated from paged pool. Not a user-mode library; the README says user-mode (TestUm) timings cannot be trusted.
caveats: Very new, single-author exploration ('not strictly benchmark-driven during its design'); no repetition counts or variance reported, compiler flags not stated, and throughput comes from a multi-threaded harness built to saturate the memory bus, so GB/s figures are aggregate and not per-call latency. The CRT baseline measures only 1.35-1.67 GB/s on the VMware guest for small to large buffers and to 0.21-0.37 GB/s on dense mismatches, which reflects that CRT implementation, not glibc/musl (glibc uses a two-way algorithm for long needles). Loses to CRT on tiny and small buffers. Kernel driver telemetry only; no independent reproduction.

name: STOKE
baseline: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 compiled x86-64 code (output quality); expert hand-written assembly for some kernels; Google Native Client's shipped libc string functions in the 2017 paper
workload: Runtime of superoptimized loop-free x86-64 kernels (OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication, Hacker's Delight, SAXPY, linked-list traversal) starting from llvm -O0 code, and 13 libc string functions from NaCl newlib.
claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2013 paper (PDF opened): the Montgomery multiplication kernel from OpenSSL's big-number library is 16 lines shorter and 1.6x faster than gcc -O3 output and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly; across the benchmark kernels STOKE matches gcc -O3 and icc -O3 starting from llvm -O0 and in several cases exceeds both. ASPLOS 2017 paper (PDF opened): 'median and average speedup of 25% over the libraries shipped by Google' for 13 libc string functions with formal verification. README tutorial: popcount drops from about 1.05 s to about 0.13 s versus a g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline build.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 baselines (versions not stated in the extracted paper text); gcc-4.9 used in the 2017 paper's translation mode; README tutorial uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline
hardware: ASPLOS 2013: synthesis and optimization on a cluster of 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons (machine used for the runtime speedups not identified in the extracted text); ASPLOS 2017: machines with two Intel Xeon E5-2667v2 3.3 GHz processors and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and Intel-microarchitecture oriented. Needs test cases plus bounded or SMT-based equivalence checking, search budgets of tens of minutes per kernel on a cluster, and works best on short loop-free sequences. README: 'STOKE isn't production ready' and 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it says it is 'not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code'.
caveats: Speedups are on hand-picked small kernels, and the ASPLOS 2013 Figure 11 reports speedup over llvm -O0 with STOKE 'comparable' to gcc -O3 and icc -O3 on many kernels, not always faster. The 2017 baseline is Google's shipped NaCl libc code (already constrained by SFI alignment rules), not a plain gcc -O3 build. A 2022 TU Delft bachelor thesis, seen only as a WebSearch snippet (not opened), reports that STOKE often fails to match gcc -O3 and struggles with loops. Not a benchmark of assemble time. Same repo holds both papers (docs/papers/asplos13.pdf, asplos17.pdf, cacm16.pdf and others).

claimed_speedup: Deserialize, SWAR mode vs built-in JSON in V8: 1,321 vs 568 MB/s (1.1 kB payload), 5,734 vs 1,295 MB/s (5.5 kB payload), 2,196 vs 168 MB/s (108 B payload), 1,056 vs 401 MB/s (52 B alphabet string). Library comparison on a 5 KiB GitHub-repo payload (deserialize): json-as struct 5,636 MB/s, native JSON 547 MB/s, fast-json-parse 547 MB/s, assemblyscript-json 32 MB/s. Smallest-gain row: 3D Vector (19 B) deserialize, 356-444 vs 83 MB/s across the three typed modes, while the dynamic JSON.Obj path ties built-in JSON on that row (82 vs 83 MB/s). tradeoffs: Typed, schema-driven (struct) API: the build-time transform generates a specialised serializer per @json class, so it only competes with JSON.parse when the schema is known up front; dynamic JSON.Obj path is slower. Needs AssemblyScript toolchain and a Wasm host; builds use --noAssert and --uncheckedBehavior always, which removes bounds and assert checks. SIMD mode needs Wasm SIMD support.
caveats: Chart values are only in PNG/SVG images (read from the PNG), not in a text table. The JS baseline parses to generic JavaScript objects while json-as parses into typed structs, so work done differs. Against Node crypto at 1,000,000 bytes: md5 698 ops/s and sha1 966 ops/s vs xxhash-wasm 64-bit 8,632 ops/s.
hardware: Not stated for the xxhashjs table; the Node crypto comparison table says an x64 MacBook Pro running Node 17.3

caveats: First-party README numbers with the hardware missing for the main table; it compares only against a slow pure-JS library that emulates 64-bit integers, not against a native xxHash binding or the C reference (the xxHash C library is already catalogued). Node crypto rows compare a non-cryptographic hash against md5/sha1, which is not like for like. name: wasman
baseline: wazero v1.12 (interpreter mode and compiler mode); also wagon v0.4 and life
workload: Go benchmarks over tiny hand-written .wat modules: Fib(20) recursive, 100k-iteration Sum loop, 64KiB MemRW, module Instantiate (decode+validate+instantiate), plus JIT-mode kernels Sort (10k i32 quicksort), Dispatch (br_table), Hash, Mandel, Indirect (call_indirect).
claimed_speedup: Interpreter vs wazero interpreter (Apple M3, ns/op): Fib 974,787 vs 1,787,663; Sum 3,014,618 vs 3,930,498; MemRW 4,751,546 vs 5,153,545; Instantiate 2,129 vs 14,100; README says 1.1-1.8x faster than wazero's interpreter, 1.5-2.4x faster than wagon, about 2x faster than life, instantiation 3-14x faster. JIT vs wazero compiler: MemRW 39,575 vs 70,643, Sort 367,952 vs 477,368, Sum 27,112 vs 26,850 (level), Fib 41,187 vs 37,832 (slower), Indirect 3,926,713 vs 2,812,512 (1.4x slower); on dual EPYC 7K62 Sum 2.0x and MemRW 1.6x ahead of wazero compiler, Fib 1.6x behind.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.24; go test -bench . -benchmem ./bench (default Go flags); fixtures compiled from .wat with wat2wasm and checked in; every run checked for the correct result before timing.
hardware: Apple M3 (main tables); dual AMD EPYC 7K62 server for the amd64 JIT comparison
tradeoffs: Pure Go with zero dependencies (no cgo), interpreter by default; optional tiered JIT (EnableJIT) only on arm64 and amd64 and per-function interpreter fallback (optimizing tier covers about 86% of spec-suite function bodies). The README claims full official spec-suite conformance, metering and interruption support.
caveats: Self-benchmarked by the project author; single run per row (no variance reported); very small workloads (Fib(20) is about 13k calls), so results may not transfer to real modules. Only Go engines were compared: cgo runtimes (wasmtime-go, wasmer-go) were deliberately excluded, so there is no comparison with wasmtime, wasmer, V8 or WAMR. The JIT result is mixed: ahead of wazero's compiler on memory-bound code, level on arithmetic, behind on recursion and call_indirect. Wazero is the Go incumbent but not one of the listed baselines.

name: Cage (wasmtime-mte, MTE-based memory safety and bounds checking for 64-bit Wasm)
baseline: Wasmtime sandboxing of 64-bit (memory64) WebAssembly with software bounds checks (inferred from the abstract wording, paper not opened)
workload: C/C++ programs compiled to 64-bit Wasm and run on real Arm hardware with MTE and PAC; Cage offloads the sandbox bounds check to Arm Memory Tagging Extension hardware.
claimed_speedup: README abstract: 'minimal runtime (<5.8%) and memory (<5.3%) overheads' for added memory safety, 'and a speedup of over 5.1%' of the sandboxing mechanism; the BibTeX abstract on the same page says memory overhead <3.7%.
compiler_and_flags: LLVM fork (TUM-DSE/llvm-memsafe-wasm) and wasi-libc fork; flags not stated on the pages opened
hardware: Real Arm hardware with MTE and PAC; CPU model not named on the pages opened
tradeoffs: Needs Arm CPUs with MTE and PAC, 64-bit Wasm (memory64) modules, and the authors' forks of LLVM, wasmtime, wasm-tools and wasi-libc; the wasmtime fork carries the upstream Apache-2.0 LICENSE file but cage-meta has no LICENSE file. Primary purpose is memory safety; the speedup is a side effect of replacing software bounds checks.
caveats: The CGO 2025 paper (doi 10.1145/3696443.3708920, pp. 538-552) and arXiv 2408.11456 were not reachable here, so numbers come from the cage-meta README only. The 5.1% figure is a small speedup of the sandboxing mechanism against software bounds checks, not a general runtime win, and the identity of the baseline build is inferred. The README abstract (memory overhead <5.3%) and BibTeX abstract (<3.7%) disagree. wasmtime-mte is a fork that tracks upstream wasmtime but is not upstreamed. Artifact on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.13772996) was not opened.

name: VectorVisor (GPU binary translator for WebAssembly)
baseline: Wasmtime running the same Wasm module on CPU (run_benchmarks_aws.py starts the CPU side with 'vectorvisor ... --wasmtime=true'), plus native x86 builds
workload: Serverless-style benchmarks (scrypt, pbkdf2, imageblur, imagehash, genpdf, lz4 compression, nlp, average) run as thousands of concurrent Wasm instances on a GPU versus CPU instances.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on the repo pages opened. README: running many copies of single-threaded Wasm on a GPU is 'ultimately improving the throughput of applications that would otherwise run on CPUs'; it also admits it is 'less efficient than manual translation'. The quantified results are in the USENIX ATC 2023 paper (not opened).
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release; benchmark Wasm built in optimized and interleaved variants (scrypt-opt-*.wasm)
hardware: AWS GPU instances with NVIDIA T4 and A10G (g4dn, g5) and an AMD Radeon Pro V520; CPU baseline instances Intel or AMD (exact CPU model not opened)
tradeoffs: Needs an OpenCL 1.2+ GPU; best on NVIDIA under Linux, AMD ROCm sometimes crashes and Intel fails beyond smoke tests; workloads must be throughput-oriented (many independent requests), single-threaded Wasm, with fixed heap and stack sizes; latency per request is higher than on CPU.
caveats: Evidence is a peer-reviewed paper (USENIX ATC 2023) plus an artifact harness, but no speedup figure could be quoted from opened pages: usenix.org was unreachable and the repo has figures (latency_throughput.png) and raw result directories but no text summary. The Wasmtime baseline is VectorVisor's own embedded --wasmtime mode on CPU, inferred from the benchmark script, not the standalone wasmtime CLI. Cost per request versus CPU instances is a different axis than a pure runtime speedup. Reproduction takes about 24 hours on AWS per the README.

name: KinoWASM (KinoRuntime)
baseline: WAMR iwasm fast interpreter (also compared against wasm3)
workload: CoreMark 1.0 compiled to a WASI wasm module (Clang 11.0.0, -O3) and a recursive fibonacci(40) module, each run through the runtime's own CLI; interpreter versus interpreter.
claimed_speedup: CoreMark Iterations/Sec: KinoRuntime 4385.746651, wasm3 3555.555556, iwasm (WAMR fast interpreter) 1734.417344; page states approximately 1.23x wasm3 and 2.53x iwasm. fibonacci(40): KinoRuntime 1838.94 ms, wasm3 2601.12 ms, iwasm 4298.94 ms; page states approximately 1.41x wasm3 and 2.34x iwasm.
compiler_and_flags: Guest module: Clang 11.0.0 (LLVM 176249bd6732), -O3. Runtime executables: KinoRuntime 'standard Clang build' with compiler version and preset not recorded; wasm3 version and build configuration not recorded; iwasm in fast-interpreter mode. Public build needs MSVC 14.50+ or clang-cl (guaranteed tail calls via musttail) with AVX2 enabled.
hardware: Intel Core i7-13700F, Windows 11 (user-reported)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; the README says it ships in several production console titles (console integrations are private)
tradeoffs: Interpreter (register-TOS, direct-threaded, tail calls), so far slower than JIT/AOT engines such as wasmtime or wasmer. Public repo builds only for Windows x64 and needs a compiler with guaranteed tail calls. No SIMD execution, no threads/atomics, no GC; WASI only partial; memory64 and exception handling partial. Host-controlled suspend/resume of guest execution is a feature. Embedding needs a host-provided linear-memory backend.
caveats: benchmark.md calls the numbers 'user-supplied measurements' and a 'preliminary snapshot': only one machine, runtime versions and compiler flags not recorded, workload binaries and CoreMark not bundled, iwasm ran 30,000 iterations while the other two ran 60,000, and the final CRC differs between iwasm (0x5275) and wasm3/KinoRuntime (0xbd59). The page itself says the metadata is insufficient for a fully documented CoreMark result. Fibonacci timing uses the in-guest clock via the runtime's WASI clock. wasm3 on Windows may be disadvantaged by its calling convention (the stitch README makes that claim for its own Windows numbers). Project is very new (first commit 2026-09-30, about 6 commits) and written by one person.
